e-21635.knowledge_point: Identifying the Parameters of a System Given Its Phase Portrait
e-21635.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/270b7c6ff796937603596f26e70886f41438ce87c043d3a1b4fc221398b8692f.png)

 

The phase portrait for a system of linear differential equations whose matrix has two real, distinct eigenvalues is shown above.
The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_1 = [-1, \ 1]^T$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 = [1, \ 0]^T,$ respectively. 

Identify the relations between $\lambda_1,$ $\lambda_2,$ and $0.$
e-21635.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/7282a63a66c9f449844292764e4e7b6f1ec472a47ff18aa7fd0c68dbe6042dbe.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/9bff79e13c06645253e57b8e6f43689c7ce21ac818c3ffdc677e03b5a9b08eb7.png) has the equation 

$$
y= -x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/d241239c6475fbcf9559c2fcbbb8ca2805a6692fd1a9b3966fe8b38441075a4d.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/9804740137aa14411a15e6a8fce4d495527bdc1980dbd0cda294cfcf05e89dd8.png)
must approach infinity as $t \to \infty.$ So, we must have $\lambda_1 >  0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/b06ebf2f3fa8f0616092292e746e84c7e925c42d38cf1c31dc4f6edede6d001b.png) has the equation 

$$
y= 0,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/fb40117d63e76b2b2db59313b173b04a9a23ef2a28493a5041584e4c7c60c67d.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/44c8b9978f9c0db5fc39702755042f1887a95fb2034bb6b01dd8d025b589aba5.png)
must approach infinity as $t \to \infty.$ So, we must have $\lambda_2 > 0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are positive. The dominant eigenvalue is the one with the greatest magnitude.

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ as they move away from the origin, the dominant eigenvalue is $\lambda_2.$

Therefore, $\lambda_2 > \lambda_1 > 0.$

e-21634.knowledge_point: Classifying Systems of Linear Differential Equations With Distinct Real Eigenvalues
e-21634.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=9x(t)+6y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-6x(t)-6y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_1=6$ and $\lambda_2=-3,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_1 = [-2, \ 1]^T$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 = [-1, \ 2]^T,$ respectively. Complete the following statements about the system by filling in the blanks.

Identify stable and unstable lines, and classify the equilibrium point (origin).

The general solution of the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/1c9e5558e6c3c4a97881100ad5a36c5ab6b2c602eb521123371bdde9c8450a6e.png)

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/a14a160428831f0fdf8a22ebcb932e655046fe4c4e258bc0d83b25c97ecfafbb.png) has the equation 

$$
y= -\dfrac12x.

lie on that line and approach infinity as $t \to \infty.$ So, $y=-\dfrac12x$ is an unstable line.

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/01186c121850d622e0f4216bb6375f7ef11d2d4cef0dd2acf2eb8f99d2a16643.png) has the equation

The first factor tends to zero, while the second tends to infinity, so nonzero solutions in the respective families approach the origin and escape to infinity. The zero solution remains at the origin. The final diagram includes solution trajectories, making it a phase portrait.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[1,\text{ }-1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[1,\text{ }2]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}\cdot {{field-1}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}\cdot {{field-2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

observation.name: Question 1
observation.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[1,\text{ }-1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[1,\text{ }2]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}\cdot {{field-1}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}\cdot {{field-2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y={{field-3}}
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line.

decision.explanation: Each eigenvector has factor e^{λt}, giving e^{-t} and e^{2t}. The eigenvectors (1,−1) and (1,2) determine lines y=−x and y=2x. Since e^{-t} tends to 0, the first family approaches the origin.

observation.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f1335e5420fe6e475cded1092e9b1ba621e0d88f46110b69ffef5e35ed080d6e.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=2x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/a53bb4e6cd7552b92424b168d0cda90fa1085b5e72fbf8a3c37a3a948bdcf9ad.png)

after.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f1335e5420fe6e475cded1092e9b1ba621e0d88f46110b69ffef5e35ed080d6e.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=2x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/a53bb4e6cd7552b92424b168d0cda90fa1085b5e72fbf8a3c37a3a948bdcf9ad.png)

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}\cdot {{field-1}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}\cdot {{field-2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$
y={{field-3}}

${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$

content.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f1335e5420fe6e475cded1092e9b1ba621e0d88f46110b69ffef5e35ed080d6e.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=2x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/a53bb4e6cd7552b92424b168d0cda90fa1085b5e72fbf8a3c37a3a948bdcf9ad.png)

The $\text{phase portrait}$ of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/6a4c15275ba80d01a90b2e010ed95e95f9a75cfa13f8e51db3433f6356949057.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}<0
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ is the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue).

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move towards the origin.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f838a055e525a264bf36b8e0478d186fe17753bba8c0088fea01ac7c5c1f8d7a.png)

The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/6a4c15275ba80d01a90b2e010ed95e95f9a75cfa13f8e51db3433f6356949057.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}<0
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ is the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue).

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move towards the origin.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f838a055e525a264bf36b8e0478d186fe17753bba8c0088fea01ac7c5c1f8d7a.png)

The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/44d0f3d13ca03a0644b2f28df9200cd521b7b44d625f346e981d2a54165284f5.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/6a4c15275ba80d01a90b2e010ed95e95f9a75cfa13f8e51db3433f6356949057.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}<0
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ is the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue).

content.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/44d0f3d13ca03a0644b2f28df9200cd521b7b44d625f346e981d2a54165284f5.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/6a4c15275ba80d01a90b2e010ed95e95f9a75cfa13f8e51db3433f6356949057.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}<0
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ is the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue).

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move towards the origin.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f838a055e525a264bf36b8e0478d186fe17753bba8c0088fea01ac7c5c1f8d7a.png)

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/1f166fad96cd30dbc0b9cf05fdabcccd26cd68e25fc26b91ae357d4015813614.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/cbb8268b959a09af3d0b57573ff08f45a2fb87f376d87f284df49cd5094412d9.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

decision.explanation: The eigenvectors (2,1) and (−1,1) give lines y=x/2 and y=−x. Arrows on y=x/2 point away from the origin, so nonzero solutions escape to infinity and λ₁>0. Arrows on y=−x point toward the origin, so solutions approach the origin and λ₂<0.

decision.explanation: The vector (2,1) gives slope 1/2, so the line is y=x/2. Its arrows point away from the origin on both sides, implying nonzero solutions grow without bound as t→∞. Therefore λ₁>0; the zero solution remains at the origin.

observation.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/1f166fad96cd30dbc0b9cf05fdabcccd26cd68e25fc26b91ae357d4015813614.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/cbb8268b959a09af3d0b57573ff08f45a2fb87f376d87f284df49cd5094412d9.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

EXPLANATION

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form c1eλ1t[21]andc2eλ2t[−11].

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[21] has the equation y=12x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ1t[21] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ1>0.

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v2=[−11] has the equation y=−x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ2t[−11] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ2<0.

decision.explanation: The eigenvectors (2,1) and (−1,1) give lines y=x/2 and y=−x. Arrows on y=x/2 point away from the origin, so nonzero solutions escape to infinity and λ₁>0. Arrows on y=−x point toward the origin, so solutions approach the origin and λ₂<0.

after.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/1f166fad96cd30dbc0b9cf05fdabcccd26cd68e25fc26b91ae357d4015813614.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/cbb8268b959a09af3d0b57573ff08f45a2fb87f376d87f284df49cd5094412d9.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[21] has the equation y=12x, as shown below.

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/c675f557abede7c8f21eadf3fd65dbd522c5ee9ad0a4ed0a804b03f357c1dc3b.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=2x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/a25c57a021e42b2fa78b71f9ab79f0676a16f7c4f1082af0e9502d4d63ed4e46.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are negative. The eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue) is the one closest to $0.$

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{2}$ as they move towards the origin, the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior is ${\lambda }_{2}.$

Therefore, ${\lambda }_{1}<{\lambda }_{2}<0.$

EXPLANATION

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form c1eλ1t[11]andc2eλ2t[12].

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[11] has the equation y=x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[11] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ1<0.

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v2=[12] has the equation y=2x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[12] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ2<0.

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are negative. The eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue) is the one closest to 0.

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector v2 as they move towards the origin, the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior is λ2.

Therefore, λ1<λ2<0.

decision.explanation: The eigenvectors give lines y=x and y=2x. Both have inward arrows, so both eigenvalues are negative. The curved trajectories become tangent to y=2x near the origin, identifying v₂ and λ₂ as the dominant direction and eigenvalue. The dominant negative eigenvalue decays more slowly and is closer to zero, so λ₁<λ₂<0. Trajectories lying exactly on the other eigenvector line remain on that line.

decision.explanation: The vector (1,1) has slope 1, giving y=x. Arrows along this line point toward the origin on both sides, so its solutions approach the origin as t→∞. Hence e^{λ₁t} decays and λ₁<0.

decision.explanation: The vectors (1,1) and (1,2) determine lines y=x and y=2x. Arrows on both lines point toward the origin, so both exponential modes decay to zero as t→∞. Therefore λ₁<0 and λ₂<0.

observation.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/c675f557abede7c8f21eadf3fd65dbd522c5ee9ad0a4ed0a804b03f357c1dc3b.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=2x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/a25c57a021e42b2fa78b71f9ab79f0676a16f7c4f1082af0e9502d4d63ed4e46.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are negative. The eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue) is the one closest to $0.$

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{2}$ as they move towards the origin, the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior is ${\lambda }_{2}.$

Therefore, ${\lambda }_{1}<{\lambda }_{2}<0.$

EXPLANATION

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form c1eλ1t[11]andc2eλ2t[12].

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[11] has the equation y=x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[11] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ1<0.

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v2=[12] has the equation y=2x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[12] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ2<0.

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are negative. The eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue) is the one closest to 0.

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector v2 as they move towards the origin, the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior is λ2.

Therefore, λ1<λ2<0.

decision.explanation: The eigenvectors give lines y=x and y=2x. Both have inward arrows, so both eigenvalues are negative. The curved trajectories become tangent to y=2x near the origin, identifying v₂ and λ₂ as the dominant direction and eigenvalue. The dominant negative eigenvalue decays more slowly and is closer to zero, so λ₁<λ₂<0. Trajectories lying exactly on the other eigenvector line remain on that line.

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=x,

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=2x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/a25c57a021e42b2fa78b71f9ab79f0676a16f7c4f1082af0e9502d4d63ed4e46.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are negative. The eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue) is the one closest to $0.$

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{2}$ as they move towards the origin, the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior is ${\lambda }_{2}.$

Therefore, ${\lambda }_{1}<{\lambda }_{2}<0.$

after.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-6t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach the origin as as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=\frac{1}{2}x$ is $\text{a stable}$ line.

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-6t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach the origin as as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=-x$ is $\text{a stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a stable node (sink)}.$

decision.explanation: The eigenvector (1,1) gives y=x, whose mode e^{4t} grows, making it unstable. The eigenvector (−1,1) gives y=−x, whose mode e^{-2t} decays, making it stable. Opposite-sign eigenvalues make the origin a saddle point.

after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)+3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[-1,\text{ }1]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options below regarding the given system.$\,$
{{field-1}} is {{field-2}} line.

$\,$
$y=-x$ is {{field-3}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-4}}.
after.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=x$ is $\text{an unstable}$ line.

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=-x$ is $\text{a stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=x(t)+4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[-2,\text{ }1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[0,\text{ }1]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options below regarding the given system.$\,$
$y=-\frac{1}{2}x$ is {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
{{field-2}} is {{field-3}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-4}}.
after.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-\frac{1}{2}x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=-\frac{1}{2}x$ is $\text{an unstable}$ line.

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
x=0.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, $x=0$ is $\text{an unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:
